Tanuja: Paper three is done. Two hours, timed.
Elizabeth: Third one this week?
Tanuja: Monday, Wednesday, today. Every other day. Pass me the marking scheme.
Elizabeth: Why not just reread your notes? They feel nicer.
Tanuja: Nicer, yes. Look: 31 out of 40 in algebra, 14 out of 40 in mensuration. Again. My notes made me feel finished with both.
Elizabeth: Ouch. So what now?
Tanuja: Tonight is only mensuration, and the questions I lost marks on. Friday I write the next paper.
Elizabeth: Can I borrow the paper? I'll sit at the next desk and time myself.
Tanuja: Start when I say. Phones face down.
Elizabeth: Fine 🙂 but snacks after.

qa.q: How often does Tanuja write a timed paper?
qa.a: Every other day: Monday, Wednesday and today, that week.

qa.q: What does Tanuja think about rereading notes compared with the paper scores?
qa.a: Tanuja feels wary of the comfort of notes, since they made mensuration seem finished when the score of 14 out of 40 said otherwise.

qa.q: What other approach could Tanuja add alongside the mock papers, and why?
qa.a: Writing a one-page summary of each weak topic after marking would help, because choosing what matters in mensuration turns the score into targeted revision.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see Tanuja's routine at first?
qa.a: Elizabeth doubts it and asks why not reread notes, but the scores persuade Elizabeth enough to ask for the paper and time a session too.

grounding: Every alternate day the student writes a timed paper and checks it against the marking scheme, so scores show which topics slip and revision becomes targeted.

passage: I'm Anjali, and in the last month before boards Jasleen and I turned my bedroom into an exam hall every other day. Timer on the table, full three-hour paper, no notes, no phone. Then we swapped papers and marked them strictly against the marking scheme, which was humbling. After the first four papers I had a column of scores by topic, and the pattern was obvious. Organic reactions: always fine. Thermodynamics: I lost marks every single time, in the same place, the sign conventions. Before, I would have spent my evenings rereading organic because it felt good. Now I spent them on sign conventions. By the eighth paper, thermodynamics was my safest section. Strange: the mocks felt worse than rereading, but they worked.

qa.q: Where did Anjali keep losing marks in thermodynamics?
qa.a: In the same place every time, the sign conventions.

qa.q: Why did rereading organic feel good to Anjali?
qa.a: Anjali felt comfortable and confident with organic, so rereading it was soothing, even though it wasn't where marks were being lost.

qa.q: What could Anjali add to make the mocks even more useful?
qa.a: A short note after each paper on why each mark was lost, so the next practice session targets the exact slip, not just the topic.

qa.q: What might the marking be like for Jasleen?
qa.a: Jasleen practises with the marking scheme too, and may find the strict swaps humbling but useful for Jasleen's own answers.

grounding: A student recalls writing timed mock papers every other day and using the scores to target the topic that kept slipping.

Tutor's note, 22 February — Karthik, Class 12 Physics
Since 1 February Karthik has written a full timed paper every alternate day in my back room, and marked it himself with the official scheme while I watched. Eleven papers so far. He records the marks lost per topic in a table. The early papers told a clear story: optics numericals leaking marks every time, while mechanics stayed strong. He admitted he had been "resting" on mechanics before, because it felt safe. For the last ten days he has spent his non-paper days almost entirely on optics, and his optics section has gone from about half marks to nearly full. His overall score has risen from 41 to 56 out of 70. I have suggested one easy day before the exam, with no full paper.
— Bhupen

qa.q: How many papers has Karthik written so far?
How did Karthik feel about mechanics before the mock papers?
qa.a: He felt safe and comfortable with mechanics, which is why he kept resting on it.

qa.q: Why does targeting optics work better than general revision?
qa.a: The table shows optics is where marks leak, so focused practice there raises the score far more than rereading strong topics.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see Karthik's progress?
qa.a: Bhupen tracks the rise from 41 to 56 and suggests an easy day before the exam, caring about rest as well as scores.

grounding: A tutor's note shows timed mock papers every alternate day revealing which topic slips, so revision becomes targeted.
